metric.why: Transformer and switchgear lead times stretched from months to years and now gate construction schedules as hard as permits do. Lead-time surveys are published by industry groups and research firms; watch the directory sources.
metric.definition: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.

reading.body:
Critical equipment lead times, not capital or permits, now set the pace at which data centers can be built.

The definition covers order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators. Those are the components that turn a committed building into a powered one. The stated pattern is that these waits stretched from months to years, and that they now gate construction schedules as hard as permits do. Money can be raised quickly, and land can be optioned quickly, but a transformer order sits in a queue that spending does not shorten.

For AI specifically, the inclusion of high-end accelerators in the same metric matters. Compute supply and building supply are measured on one clock, which means a model cannot be served until both the chip and the electrical gear behind it arrive. A stalled switchgear order idles everything downstream of it, including the accelerators already paid for. This is why lead times belong in a financial and supply chain category alongside hyperscaler capital expenditure and colocation rental rates: they are the physical term in the cost of adding capacity.

What this does not provide is any actual figure. There is no current lead time, no historical series, no breakdown by equipment type, no vendor or regional detail, and no date attached to the shift from months to years. It establishes that the metric is tracked and why it is thought to bind, not how long the waits are today or whether they are lengthening or easing.
